extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and readers studying classical mechanics / physics
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of core classical-mechanics principles: historical measures of force, kinematic equations (constant and variable forces), units and dimensions, and the conservation laws (momentum, centre of gravity, areas) with illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descartes' definition of mv as momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: “Descartes defined mv as momentum” and treated certain propositions (e.g., “a body preserves unchanged its velocity and direction”) as self-evident a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual critique: Mach notes this is an error — such propositions should be based on experience rather than asserted a priori. Use empirical evidence (not only a priori reasoning) as the foundation for laws like inertia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leibnitz's vis viva (mv^2) as measure of force
rubrics_metrics.description: Leibnitz distinguished between simple pressure (vis mortua) and the force of a moving body (vis viva), asserting the true measure of force (in certain contexts) is determined by mv^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leibnitz argued the product of mass and the square of velocity (mv^2) is the appropriate measure in many cases (e.g., raising bodies to heights related to descent velocity); acceptance of this measure excludes perpetual motion. Note: Leibnitz did not have a fully developed concept of mass; successors associated his expressions with the notion of mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different legitimate measures of effectiveness (mv vs mv^2 vs Newtonian force)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the Cartesian measure (Σ m v) and the Leibnitzian measure (Σ m v^2) have justification in different senses; neither should be confused with the common Newtonian measure of force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret measures according to context: Cartesian and Leibnitzian measures justify different empirical/technical uses (e.g., machine equilibrium vs. work/energy). Recognize distinct physical meanings (momentum vs energy) rather than conflating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinematic equations and modification for variable forces
rubrics_metrics.description: The three fundamental equations (for rectilinear motion under constant forces) must be modified when the force is variable: for variable forces m v = ∫ p dt + C, and the second equation becomes s = ∫ t dt + Ct + D, with constants of integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations: p is the variable force, dt the time-element, ∫ p dt the sum of impulses from start to end, and constants denote initial values. Curvilinear motion is treated by resolving into three perpendicular rectilinear components; the same integral forms apply to components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneity requirement for mechanical equations
rubrics_metrics.description: “The mathematical processes of addition, subtraction, and equating possess intelligible meaning only when applied to quantities of the same kind... whether the members of the equation are quantities of the same kind, that is, whether they can be measured by the same unit, or whether... the equation is homogeneous.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always check that every term in a mechanical equation has the same dimensions (units). Do not add or equate unlike quantities (e.g., masses with times or masses with velocities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derived units and the theory of dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Derived (or absolute) units depend on arbitrary fundamental units (mass, length, time); their functional dependence is expressed as dimensions (Fourier). Example: velocity has dimensions L T^-1, acceleration L T^-2, force m L T^-2, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dimensions to define derived units consistently (e.g., unit of area = (unit length)^2). The table of names/symbols/dimensions helps verify homogeneity of formulas and to express new mechanical quantities in terms of fundamental units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using dimensions to convert numerical values between unit systems
rubrics_metrics.description: If the dimensions of a quantity are known for one set of fundamental units, the numerical value in another set is found from the dimensions. Example: acceleration scales as (length_unit)/(time_unit^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the dimensional scaling law: when unit length changes by factor A and unit time by r, acceleration's numerical value changes by (r^2 / A). Example given: 9.81 (m/s^2) becomes 35.316 (km/min^2) when switching units appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: International prototypes and practical issues of standards
rubrics_metrics.description: International Bureau standards: unit of length — the International Metre (distance between engraved lines on prototype platino-iridium bar); unit of mass — the International Prototype Kilogram (platinum cylinder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical notes on reproducibility and historical difficulties (e.g., damage to earlier standards, thermometer construction affecting temperature marks). Awareness that national practice (British, American) may vary and that conversion/comparison must account for such subtleties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute (CGS) vs gravitational systems of measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute system (e.g., Centimetre-Gramme-Second) defines units independent of local gravity; gravitational system uses kilogram or pound-weight as unit of force and foot-pound or kilogramme-metre as energy units, which depends on local g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In CGS: dyne = g·cm/s^2, erg = g·cm^2/s^2, etc. In gravitational system, reconcile units by adjusting mass unit (mass = weight/g) or choosing a time unit so that local g is unity; be aware of variations of g between locations (Paris vs Washington examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of conservation of momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: The momentum (Σ m v) of a system is determined exclusively by external forces; internal forces between parts cancel by Newton's third law, so internal forces have no influence on the total impulse or momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate conservation by resolving forces and velocities into orthogonal components; the sum of impulses in each direction equals the momentum generated in that direction. Use sign conventions for opposite directions. Apply to interacting masses and systems to predict resultant motion (or lack thereof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of conservation of the centre of gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of a system cannot be displaced by mutual action of its parts; the motion of the centre of gravity is determined solely by external forces. Coordinates: x̄ = Σ m x / Σ m, and acceleration of the centre cp = Σ m φ / M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation and examples: an animal cannot move its centre of gravity without external supports; throwing stones from a vehicle causes opposite vehicle motion so overall centre remains fixed; cannon recoil follows MV + mv = 0; for systems, the centre moves exactly as if all mass and forces concentrated at that point. Use Σmφ/M to compute centre acceleration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of areas (mentioned)
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed among the laws: conservation of momentum, of the centre of gravity, and of areas (header).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chunk names conservation of areas as one of the principal rules developed for routine treatment of mechanical problems; detailed exposition appears elsewhere (not elaborated in this excerpt).
